paragraph:
Blooms, booms and busts
Four centuries of speculative frenzies, from Dutch tulips to artificial intelligence, hold uncomfortable lessons for today's investors
In the first week of February 1637 an auctioneer in a Haarlem tavern held up a lot of tulip bulbs and waited for a bid that never came. Within days the trade that the Dutch had nicknamed windhandel, or “dealing in wind”, had seized up, and contracts struck at fantastical prices, scratched with a (nib) in (crabbed) handwriting, were worth little more than the paper they were written on. The object of all this passion was an (exotic) import from the Ottoman empire, a flower prized at the sultan's court long before it was (cultivated) in Dutch gardens. It was an odd thing on which to stake a fortune. Unlike the (gardenia), whose heavy (aroma) can fill a room, most tulips are all but (unscented); a nation in search of something (aromatic) to obsess over could have done better. What made a tulip (celebrated) was its looks, and above all the (striated) petals of the so-called “broken” varieties, flamed with (magenta), purple or crimson on a white ground as if painted by hand.
Only in the 1920s did botanists work out what caused those flames: a virus, spread by aphids, that broke the pigment into a (mosaic) of streaks and sapped the bulb's strength. The most coveted tulips, in other words, were sick. Their beauty was a symptom, and their weakness, a kind of botanical (anemia), meant that they multiplied slowly, keeping supply scarce and prices (bloated). The rarest of them all, the Semper Augustus, white flamed with red, was reputedly offered for the price of a (majestic) house on an Amsterdam canal. Some 240 years later Gerard Manley Hopkins would give thanks for (dappled) things, for skies two-toned like a (brindled) cow; the tulip fanciers of Haarlem, who paid most for blooms that were (piebald) and (maculated), had got there first. It is hard to imagine a better emblem of a bubble: an asset whose (characteristic) allure was inseparable from a hidden disease, admired for an (aesthetic) whose cause nobody understood.
Most of what the world thinks it knows about tulip (mania) comes from Charles Mackay, a Scottish journalist whose “Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds” first appeared in 1841. The book is an (encyclopedia) of folly with an (eclectic) range, in which alchemists, fortune-tellers, crusaders and haunted houses jostle with financial bubbles, and its stories have taken on the (patina) of age. Mackay tells of a sailor who mistook a precious bulb for an onion and ate it with his herring: surely the costliest breakfast in history and, given what tulip bulbs do to the (gastric) lining, not a pleasant one. He tells of (stolid) burghers ruined and a nation (possessed). The sailor's breakfast is now pub (trivia), but much of the rest belongs to the (apocrypha) of finance. Historians who have since combed the Dutch archives, notably Anne Goldgar, find scant evidence of the ruin Mackay described. He leaned heavily on (moralistic) pamphlets published after the crash by authors with a (didactic) purpose and a weakness for (melodrama). The true (saga) was smaller and more (prosaic): a (sporadic) trade, confined largely to merchants and prosperous artisans, that barely dented the Dutch economy.
Yet the myth has outlived the facts, because it is useful. Every boom needs a cautionary tale, and every (cynic) needs a (barb) to hurl at the bulls. Mackay's (pharisaic) tone, which treats greed as a failing of other people, can seem (anachronistic) today. His central insight does not: that men, as he put it, go mad in herds and recover their senses only slowly, one by one.
Eighty-three years after Haarlem the madness crossed the North Sea. In 1720 London went wild for the South Sea Company, which had swapped a large chunk of the national debt for a monopoly on trade with Spain's American colonies, a trade that the Spanish crown kept on a tight leash. Its shares rose roughly eightfold in the first half of the year, and an (armada) of copycat schemes set sail in its wake. Even the (phlegmatic) English began to (succumb) to the fever. In the coffee houses of Exchange Alley a clerk leaning against a door (jamb) could make a fortune before lunch, and (unprincipled) promoters raised money for everything from perpetual-motion wheels to, legend has it, “an undertaking of great advantage, but nobody to know what it is”. The South Sea Company itself lobbied for the Bubble Act of June 1720, which sought to (forbid) joint-stock companies without a royal charter: less a blow against speculation than an attempt to (shield) its own share price from rivals.
Isaac Newton, master of the Royal Mint and no (untutored) investor, sold early at a profit, bought back near the top and lost a fortune, reckoned at some £20,000. His (purported) lament, that he could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies but not the madness of people, may be legend; the losses were real. By the end of the year the shares had (shed) most of their gains. A parliamentary inquiry uncovered a (sordid) trail of bribes to ministers, and the chancellor of the exchequer was sent to the Tower. It became fashionable to (upbraid) the (lowbred) stockjobbers who had grown rich overnight, though plenty of dukes had joined the scramble. Street hawkers sold (ribald) verses, and (vinegared) pamphleteers portrayed Exchange Alley as a (depraved) den of thieves. William Hogarth produced a crowded, (panoramic) engraving, as (emblematic) of its age as any image of the century, in which a (diabolic) figure hacks Fortune to pieces and flings the chunks to the mob while citizens of every rank ride a merry-go-round.
Across the Channel, France was in the grip of something stranger still. John Law, a (peripatetic) Scottish gambler with a (checkered) past, who had killed a man in a duel in London and escaped from prison, talked his way into control of French finances. His schemes had a whiff of (megalomania): a national bank issuing paper money, a single company to monopolize colonial trade and swallow the national debt, and the promise of riches from Louisiana, where his Mississippi Company founded New Orleans in 1718 on the river's swampy (delta). Colonists, some of them convicts shipped out against their will, died in their hundreds in the (fetid) (miasma) of the swamps. In the rue Quincampoix, the narrow Paris street where shares changed hands, a hunchback reputedly rented out his back as a writing desk. When a decree in May 1720 set out to halve the value of shares and banknotes, the fury was such that the government had to (countermand) it within a week. Confidence was never (restored), and Law fled France in disgrace. He died in poverty in Venice in 1729 and is buried a short walk from the (piazza) of San Marco.
Britain's Victorians, so (staid) in the popular imagination, were in fact (prolific) speculators. In the 1840s they poured their savings into railways, and Parliament authorized thousands of miles of new track, much of it duplicating lines already built. George Hudson, the “Railway King”, was hailed as a genius, and the press hung a (garland) of superlatives around his neck until it emerged that his (underhanded) accounting had paid dividends out of capital. His admirers (deserted) him, and he spent years abroad dodging creditors. The boom was hardly an (unqualified) success for investors, and the (dilapidated) stations of redundant lines that never paid their way still dot the countryside. Yet it left something valuable behind: the skeleton of Britain's railway network, built with money that its backers never got back. The (sequela) of that particular fever was, unusually, a healthy one.
The same decades produced pteridomania, a craze for ferns and their (serrated) fronds that was named by the novelist Charles Kingsley, and “orchidelirium”, in which collectors paid fortunes for specimens of tropical (flora) and sent (intrepid) hunters to Colombia and Borneo, some of whom died of fever in pursuit of a single (orchid). Others fell for phrenology, which claimed to read character from the (cephalic) bumps beneath the scalp, or for mesmerism, whose (hypnotic) performers drew (packed) halls. Francis Galton, Darwin's half-cousin, gave the world the (eugenic) dream that would curdle into something (horrific) in the century that followed. Gilbert and Sullivan, who knew their audience, wrote an (operetta) in which a South Seas island kingdom converts itself into a limited-liability company, so that should it fail, nobody need pay. It remains the most (comic) explanation of the corporate form, and among the most (pellucid).
America's turn came in the 1920s. Radio was the miracle technology of the age, every rooftop seemed to sprout an (antenna), and the Radio Corporation of America was the market's darling. Small investors bought on margin, sometimes putting down a tenth of the price, and the riskiest stocks traded on an exchange whose brokers had done business outdoors, on the (curb) of Broad Street, until 1921. Pools of speculators drove prices up and down at will; the bear (raid) was a favorite (tactic). In Florida, (humid) swampland changed hands as fast as it could be surveyed, often between buyers who never saw a (deed), until a hurricane in 1926 finished the boom off. When the stockmarket crashed in October 1929, RCA began a slide that would wipe out almost all of its value. John Kenneth Galbraith, whose history of the crash remains the most (acerbic), later wrote a short history of financial (euphoria) in which he blamed, above all, the brevity of the financial memory: a collective (amnesia) that lets each generation discover for itself the joys of leverage.
After the war the pattern recurred with (kaleidoscopic) variety. The “go-go” fund managers of the 1960s piled into conglomerates that promised to (weld) unrelated businesses into (synergic) wholes; the savings seldom materialized. In the early 1970s the “Nifty Fifty”, blue chips deemed so safe that they need never be sold, were savaged in the bear market of 1973-74. On a single day in October 1987 the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 22.6%, and the Federal Reserve's (improvised) promise of liquidity taught investors a lesson they have never forgotten. A decade later Long-Term Capital Management, whose partners included two Nobel laureates and whose models drew on an option-pricing (formula) that had helped win them the prize, lost $4.6bn in a few months and had to be rescued by its creditors.
In Tokyo at the end of the 1980s, it was said, the grounds of the Imperial Palace were worth more than all the land in California, a calculation widely repeated and never properly (verified). When Japan's bubble (deflated), it did so slowly and painfully. Banks kept (indebted) zombie firms alive, savers were (repressed) by near-zero interest rates, and an economy (blighted) by bad debts and falling prices became a byword for stagnation. The Nikkei took 34 years to regain its 1989 peak.
The dotcom boom of the late 1990s supplied the modern template. Pets.com, an online pet-supply shop with a (sarcastic) sock puppet as its (figurehead), went public in February 2000 and was liquidated nine months later; a more (bathetic) mascot for an era would be hard to invent, though the puppet is now an object of (nostalgia). AOL and Time Warner announced a (star-crossed) merger in January 2000 that turned into an (unmitigated) disaster. Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve, had warned of “irrational exuberance” in 1996, in typically (gnomic) fashion, and then watched shares rise for more than three years. Telecoms firms laid enough fiber-optic cable to circle the globe many times over; after the bust much of it lay dark, (underutilized) for years, while the industry limped along in a (ragged) state until a new generation of internet firms snapped up the capacity at knock-down prices. There followed years of corporate (anorexia), in which chastened firms cut investment to the bone and hoarded cash.
The bubble that burst in 2007-08 was different in kind, because it was built on debt. American mortgages were sliced, pooled and repackaged into securities so (convoluted) that even (sophisticated) buyers could not say what they held, and the prospectuses for (esoteric) creations such as the CDO-squared ran to hundreds of pages of (hieroglyphic) legalese. Triple-A ratings made the paper look (ironclad). The risks were (calculated), modeled and, as it turned out, (underestimated) by orders of magnitude, thanks to an (astigmatic) view of correlation which assumed that house prices could not fall everywhere at once. In July 2007 the boss of Citigroup remarked that as long as the music was playing, bankers had to get up and dance. Two months later depositors were queuing beneath the (fascia) of Northern Rock's branches in Britain's first bank run in well over a century.
A financial system stuffed with leverage behaves like a body with (hemophilia): a small cut bleeds and bleeds. When Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008, credit markets froze, and firms that relied on short-term funding faced something close to (asphyxia). Subprime loans that had looked like a scratch turned (septic). Regulators, who had (assured) the world that risk had been safely dispersed, had been (myopic) beforehand and were (flustered) afterwards; they proved a broken (reed). Teams of (forensic) accountants spent years picking through the wreckage, and prosecutors served many a (subpoena), but few senior bankers went to jail. Each generation, it seems, must pick at the (scab) for itself.
Cheap money and the (pandemic) of 2020, which confined millions of bored people at home with stimulus checks and trading apps, produced a carnival. Blank-check companies raised record sums. Retail traders who called themselves “apes” organized online like a (militia) and squeezed hedge funds that had bet against GameStop, an ailing video-game retailer. Cryptocurrencies multiplied into a (plethora) of tokens, many of them jokes that became serious money, launched with white papers as (runic) as a Viking gravestone and (cryptic) to the (uninitiated). Bitcoin's most (fanatic) holders prize it for its scarcity, much as collectors prize a rare coin; its appeal is partly (numismatic). Cartoon apes sold as digital collectibles for millions of dollars. Back in 2017 a maker of iced tea had renamed itself Long Blockchain and watched its shares soar: blockchain was the (fad) of the moment. In 2022 a crypto exchange whose founder had presented himself as an (altruistic) billionaire collapsed; its success turned out to rest on the (barefaced) misuse of customers' money, and he was convicted the following year. The jargon of investment banking gave way to the (demotic) slang of Reddit, and deception, as in every boom, proved (endemic).
Economists have spent decades trying to classify these (phenomena). Charles Kindleberger, building on the work of Hyman Minsky, described a sequence in which a “displacement”, such as a new technology, a war or a financial innovation, kindles a boom; credit expands, prices rise and the boom feeds on itself until it turns (frenetic). Insiders take their profits and outsiders pile in; then something, often trivial, pricks the bubble and the sequence runs in reverse, through distress and panic to what Kindleberger called “revulsion”. Minsky's insight was that stability is itself destabilizing: long periods of calm breed complacency, and complacency breeds leverage. Keynes likened professional investment to a newspaper beauty contest in which the aim is to pick not the prettiest face but the one the other judges will pick, and saw markets as (animated) less by cold arithmetic than by “animal spirits”. An (epidemic) of speculation, on this view, is (episodic) but never cured.
Sociologists and behavioral economists have filled in the picture. David Riesman described the (other-directed) personality, who steers by radar, watching what the neighbors are doing, rather than by an inner gyroscope. Harvey Leibenstein contrasted the bandwagon effect, in which people want something because others have it, with the (snob) effect, in which they want it because others do not; tulips, like the hottest private shares today, managed to excite both. Jack Guttentag and Richard Herring coined the term “disaster (myopia)” for the tendency to underweight rare catastrophes the longer it has been since the last one. Investors, like a shoal of (scad) wheeling as one, find safety in numbers right up to the moment when numbers become the danger, and then follow the (pied) piper of the day out of the market as eagerly as they followed him in. Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff gave their (encyclopedic) study of eight centuries of financial crises a title that could serve as an epitaph for all of them: “This Time Is Different”.
Which brings us to artificial intelligence. The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was a (watershed), and investors have since poured money into anything connected with AI with an enthusiasm that recalls every episode above. It is (chic) for any company to have an AI strategy, and AI now tops every boardroom (agenda). Yet the bulls have a strong case, and an (evenhanded) assessment must begin with it. Unlike Pets.com, the firms at the center of the boom are among the most profitable in history. Nvidia, the 800-pound (gorilla) of the chip world, has enjoyed a (meteoric) rise, becoming in 2025 the first company to be valued at $4trn and then $5trn, and its quarterly results have become a (bravura) performance that markets await like the opening night of an opera. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta earn (superb) profits from older businesses and can afford to spend them. P.T. Barnum once exhibited a Feejee (mermaid), the torso of a monkey stitched to the tail of a fish, to crowds who paid to be fooled. Nobody seriously thinks AI is that kind of (hybrid): the technology is (authentic), and its uses are real.
Models write code, summarize contracts and help people with (dyslexia) read and write. An AI system that predicts the shapes of proteins won its creators a share of the Nobel prize in chemistry in 2024; others help chemists design antibiotics against drug-resistant (bacteria), sift (genetic) data, detect (somatic) mutations in tumors and flag (arrhythmic) heartbeats in electrocardiograms. Millions of people confide in chatbots for something close to (therapeutic) conversation, not always wisely. The (linguistic) fluency of large language models would have astonished computer scientists a decade ago, and speech-recognition systems that once stumbled over (phonetic) ambiguities now cope with thick regional accents. Voice-cloning tools can produce a convincing (replica) of anyone's voice from a few seconds of audio. The (disembodied) voices of AI assistants are acquiring bodies, too: startups promise (anthropoid) robots that stride about like any other (biped) and lift like a stevedore, while (quadruped) robot dogs already inspect oil rigs. A robot arm with a (spatula) flips burgers in a few American kitchens; in warehouses, driverless forklifts slide their (tined) arms under pallets without a human in sight.
Creative work is not spared. Image generators have alarmed (graphic) designers, and in 2024 record labels sued two AI music startups, alleging that they had trained their models on copyrighted recordings. Machines have (composed) passable pastiches of a Mozart (sonata) and a Bach (cantata); they can sing an (aria) in a (full-bodied) baritone without the expense of an (orchestra), knock out a pop (ballad) over (acoustic) guitar, or write a poem one (stanza) at a time. Video models can conjure a (ballerina) pirouetting on a frozen lake. Some of the business plans built on all this read like a (fantasia) on a theme by Silicon Valley.
The scale of the build-out is (titanic). The biggest tech firms are spending several hundred billion dollars a year on data centers and the (specialized) chips that fill them, an investment boom that by some estimates accounted for much of America's economic growth in 2025. Investors' appetite has been (catholic): chipmakers, utilities, cooling specialists, even uranium miners have been swept up. William Blake's dark (satanic) mills have found a successor in the data center, a (drab), windowless box in which (serried) ranks of servers hum on a concrete (slab) the size of several football fields, while a steel (scaffold) for the next one rises alongside. Tax breaks have lured them deep into the (rustic) (hinterland) of (landlocked) states such as Iowa, where (unspoiled) farmland now sprouts substations; the ethanol craze of 2006, when every (cob) in the state seemed destined for a fuel tank, looks quaint by comparison. Others cluster where the climate helps: in Sweden's far north, where (arctic) air cools the halls and engineers swap the fleece vest for a (parka), or on Iceland's Reykjanes (peninsula), where (lava) has burst through the ground repeatedly in recent years and geothermal plants supply the power. Microsoft once sank a capsule full of servers off the Orkney islands to see whether computers could thrive in an (aquatic) habitat; they did, though the project was quietly shelved. Elsewhere they are rising on a sun-baked (mesa) in the American south-west, where cooling systems compete with farmers for water in (arid) country.
The chip factories that feed them are more (aseptic) than any operating room, because a speck of dust can ruin a wafer of (microscopic) transistors. Taiwan, which makes the bulk of the world's most advanced chips, is the (aorta) of the whole enterprise, and it sits within easy range of Chinese missiles. America's export controls have spawned a lively trade in (contraband) chips smuggled to China through third countries, and a plan to ration exports with a country-by-country (quota), unveiled in January 2025, was scrapped within months. Supply remains (constrained), and (demand) for electricity is such that power companies are scrambling for gas turbines and even working to restart a shuttered reactor at Three Mile Island. In Memphis, turbines installed to power one AI supercomputer drew protests from neighborhoods already burdened with high rates of (asthma). And three centuries after John Law sold shares in the riches of Louisiana, one of the world's largest AI data centers is rising on former farmland in a (bucolic) corner of the same state, financed in large part with debt held in a special-purpose vehicle off its owner's balance-sheet. History, it seems, has a sense of humor.
The bears' worry is less the technology than the money. Revenues from AI are growing fast but remain (anemic) relative to spending; by one widely cited reckoning from a venture-capital firm, the industry needs hundreds of billions of dollars a year in new revenue to justify its outlays, and is nowhere near that. Chips that are cutting-edge today will be (superannuated) within a few years, and skeptics who pore over every (minutia) of the tech giants' accounts argue that generous depreciation schedules flatter profits in ways that are (unjustified). In 2025 a web of deals, with chipmakers investing in AI labs that then buy their chips and cloud providers taking stakes in their own customers, drew comparisons with the vendor financing that inflated the telecoms bubble. Drawing a (schematic) of who owes what to whom would tax the patience of an (arachnid), and the risks are (manifold). The AI economy is arranged in (concentric) circles, with chipmakers at the core, cloud giants around them and a (penumbra) of startups at the edge, and a shock at the edge would travel inward.
Increasingly the build-out is financed with borrowing, through bonds, private credit and leases, and that matters, because the most destructive bubbles are those built on debt. An equity bubble that bursts leaves shareholders (numb) and poorer; a debt bubble can leave the banking system in a (coma). Pension funds and insurers have (committed) billions to private-credit funds, which are lightly regulated, and many still hold (uncommitted) capital looking for a home. Risks tend to accumulate (unnoticed) in the (unregulated) corners of finance, which is where much of this lending now sits. The tech giants, (drenched) in cash, could survive a bust; the same cannot be said of some of the developers that build data centers on borrowed money for tenants who may one day walk away.
Prices, meanwhile, have become (detached) from earnings in places. Charts of some AI-linked stocks trace a near-perfect (parabola), and valuations of companies with barely an (iota) of revenue have grown (tumid). A handful of tech giants now account for a share of America's stockmarket that is (unprecedented) in modern times, and the concentration is so (pronounced) that a portfolio which simply tracks the index is close to (monochromatic): a single bet on a single theme in a (lopsided) market. Index funds buy whatever is big, so (inertia) pushes ever more money into the giants. Investors who want still more exposure can buy (thematic) exchange-traded funds; investors who want less find little shelter.
The fear of missing out, a very modern (phobia), has been (institutionalized). A fund manager who shuns AI stocks and lags the index risks losing her job, which makes the index a (despotic) master. In boardrooms, (paranoia) about being left behind, a creed that Intel's Andy Grove once preached, drives ever larger capital budgets. It has become (impolitic) in Silicon Valley to say the word “bubble” aloud; the (heretic) who does so is told that he does not understand exponential curves, and bulls dismiss doubters as (unenlightened). Executives greet the question with (studied) indifference or (emphatic) denials, and their (feigned) humility rarely conceals their (unfeigned) enthusiasm. Investors who suffer from (acrophobia) have had a miserable few years.
The (rhetoric) of the boom would be familiar to John Law. AI bosses with ample (charisma) issue (bombastic) forecasts: that superintelligence is a few years away, that AI will cure most diseases, that a (cornucopia) of cheap goods and services awaits, a (vista) of growth without end. Doomers issue (apocalyptic) warnings about the same machines, which, as a (caustic) observer might note, is another way of saying that they are extraordinarily powerful and therefore worth a great deal of money. Artificial general intelligence is offered as a (panacea) for sluggish productivity and a road to (utopia); it may yet prove a (chimera). The pursuit has a whiff of Captain Ahab's (monomania), and the (cosmic) ambitions of some founders are matched only by their (egocentric) habits. The industry's (dogma) is that scale is all you need, that bigger models trained on more data with more computing power will keep getting smarter, though that is hardly (settled) science, and AI's capabilities form a (jagged) frontier, superhuman at some tasks and hopeless at others. Selling AI shares has become (anathema) to fund managers who remember what happened to those who sold internet stocks in 1998.
AI has been here before. Twice, in the 1970s and again in the late 1980s, the field went through “AI winters”, when funding froze and research became a (tundra) of abandoned projects; a bust now would bring an (antarctic) chill to the startups at its edge. Boosters like to compare today's advances to the (neolithic) revolution, when farming transformed human life. The biologist E.O. Wilson put the danger more soberly: humanity, he said, combines (paleolithic) emotions, medieval institutions and godlike technology.
The culture that produces all this is (hermetic) and more than a little (self-absorbed). A lab's (insignia) on a hoodie has become one of the most coveted status symbols in San Francisco. Founders with (cherubic) faces and (beatific) smiles speak with (seraphic) calm of building machines cleverer than themselves, while (disheveled) engineers in their twenties field pay offers that would make a footballer blush. Talent has become (nomadic), hopping between labs in a (demented) bidding war; capital is a (nomad) too, moving to wherever the next story is. Some founders follow (ascetic) regimes, fasting for days to optimize their bodies; their conferences, by contrast, have become (sybaritic) affairs. Co-founders who fall out become (estranged) and then litigious. Their (philanthropic) pledges are generous, their (devoted) followers online are legion and their (rabid) fans are intolerant of doubt.
Venture capitalists, whose payoffs are (asymmetric) because a single hit can repay a hundred failures, are (disposed) to back long shots, and the AI labs they fund burn cash with something close to (pyromania). A startup's early life is an (anaerobic) sprint, spending faster than it can breathe in revenue until the (lactic) burn sets in. Each is a (larva) that may or may not turn into something with wings; most will (fold), as most always do. Much of the paper wealth of AI startups is, like the value of an out-of-the-money option, entirely (extrinsic): hope with a price tag. In the (prehistoric) era of computing, the late 1990s, a business plan on a napkin could raise millions; today a slide deck with “agent” on the cover can raise billions, though AI agents remain (embryonic). There are (myriad) such firms, and their valuations offer a (platonic) ideal of the growth stock: all future, no present.
Competition may be a bigger threat than any shortage of customers. In January 2025 DeepSeek, an (iconoclastic) Chinese lab, released a model that rivaled American ones at a fraction of the cost, and Nvidia lost nearly $600bn of market value in a day, a (seismic) shock by any standard. Investors greeted it with remarkable (sangfroid) and in time bought back in, treating the episode as a bear (cub) of a correction rather than the real thing. But it was a reminder that models may become (generic) commodities, and that Chinese labs, which routinely (underbid) American rivals on price, have made an (inroad) into markets that Silicon Valley assumed were its own. Talk of an AI arms race has grown (chauvinistic) on both sides of the Pacific, and (diplomatic) wrangling over chips has become a fixture of summits. Calling Nvidia the new Cisco, the darling of 2000 that lost most of its value in the bust, is a (backhanded) compliment, and investors treat a merely good quarter from the company as a personal (snub).
Silicon Valley's strength has always rested on its networks. AnnaLee Saxenian, a scholar of the region, showed how (ethnic) networks of Chinese and Indian engineers carried capital and know-how back and forth between California and Asia; those ties now run into the teeth of geopolitics. Plenty of investors claim to be (agnostic) about which model will win, buying the picks and shovels instead, while others hold an almost (mystic) faith in exponential curves. Warren Buffett's (laconic) advice, to be fearful when others are greedy, is quoted far more often than it is followed, and every (critic) of the boom is reminded that the skeptics of 1996 were more than three years early.
The boom has generated a literature of its own: founders' biographies that read as one long (panegyric), (eulogistic) magazine profiles, the occasional (vitriolic) (polemic) and the odd doorstopper of a (screed) whose back-cover (blurb) promises to explain everything. Mentions of AI on earnings calls have soared, and the calls themselves have become (long-winded), the language (florid) and (turgid) with jargon, the press releases written in (antiseptic) corporate-speak. Machines now write much of that prose, and it shows. AI-generated text is accused of being (bland) and (insipid): (hackneyed) phrases, (pleonastic) filler such as “end result”, (periphrastic) hedging and (labored) metaphors, strung together in sentences that are (mannered) or (stilted) where they should be (understated). In fairness, a model can (proofread) a prospectus in seconds and catch a missing (comma) of the kind that once cost a Maine dairy $5m in an overtime dispute. It still produces (garbled) citations and invents facts with complete (aplomb).
There is no shortage of (opinionated) commentary. Television pundits are (histrionic), podcasters (glib), the occasional executive refreshingly (candid). The (disinterested) observer, with no position to talk up, is a rare creature. An (unguarded) remark by a chief executive, or an (adlib) aside at a conference, can move a stock by billions of dollars. On trading floors the mood swings from (agitated) to (contented) and back within a morning, and markets have a (sadistic) habit of rallying just after the bears capitulate, leaving them (discomfited).
The signs of froth are there for those who look. Companies that add “AI” to their names or earnings calls see their shares jump, much as Long Blockchain's did; in 2024 American regulators fined two investment advisers for “AI washing”, overstating their use of the technology, an early (reprimand) to an industry that has been (infatuated) with the label. Quantum-computing stocks, many with scant revenue, soared on the promise of machines that must be chilled to (cryogenic) temperatures, and a decade or so earlier (quixotic) startups that planned to mine an (asteroid) for platinum attracted serious money before running out of it. Regulating AI is a (wicked) problem. Laws written for an earlier age look (antiquated), governments are (halfhearted), and labs that set up safety teams have been known to (disband) them. Some officials have made a (stab) at rules, but the (belated) reforms of one cycle tend to be fought by the lobbyists of the next.
Cheap money has fueled almost every episode. Walter Bagehot, the great Victorian editor of The Economist, whose (limpid) prose still repays reading, observed that John Bull could stand many things but not two per cent: when safe assets yield little, savers reach for riskier ones. A long era of near-zero interest rates acted as an (anesthetic) on investors' judgment. Rising prices are a powerful form of (analgesia), dulling the pain of doubt, and when they stop rising the market's favorite (analgesic) is a rate cut. Easy credit is a (narcotic); a (hypodermic) of central-bank liquidity, administered after almost every wobble since 1987, has taught markets to expect the next one. William McChesney Martin, a former chairman of the Federal Reserve, said that the central bank's job was to take away the punch bowl just as the party gets going; a market in the grip of (dipsomania) never thanks it for doing so. Today's central bankers, (even-tempered) by profession and (measured) in their language, have good reason for (insomnia). Their (graduated) approach to raising and cutting rates has (damped) volatility in the past, but it cannot repeal the cycle.
Markets that are (liquid) in good times turn (viscid) in bad ones, as buyers vanish just when sellers need them most. A (placid), even (languid) summer can give way to (hectic) autumn trading, and a (torrid) rally to a (frigid) reception for every new share issue. Valuation models assume a (static) world, but the (kinetic) energy of a market in motion is hard to stop, and when it reverses, rallies become (spasmodic), volumes (tepid), prices (depressed) and the mood (subdued). Overconfidence is (chronic) among fund managers, (choleric) traders nurse (peptic) ulcers, and the spectacle of a once-feted founder pleading with creditors is as (pathetic) as it is familiar. A (marked) slowdown in AI spending would wreak (havoc) on the suppliers that depend on it, and a business model too (rigid) to adapt would not survive; even a (muted) response from customers to a new model can do damage.
Where does this leave a (levelheaded) investor? The (dilemma) is old. Bubbles are rarely (premeditated) conspiracies; they are (unpremeditated) collective acts in which millions of (well-groomed), (informed) and otherwise (hardheaded) people persuade one another. The (wizened) veterans of 2000 and 2008 view the boom with a (jaundiced) eye; younger traders, (enamored) of the technology and (inured) to drawdowns that the central bank always seemed to reverse, are (unmoved). Both camps can be (closed-minded). The (dyspeptic) bears of the late 1990s were right in the end, but their (mistimed) bets cost them dearly in the meantime; a line usually credited to Keynes, that markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent, makes the point, though the attribution is itself (unsubstantiated). Even (jaded) analysts concede that going out on a (limb) against a (full-fledged) bubble is not for the (fainthearted), and the (stouthearted) bulls, for now, have had the better of the argument.
That argument divides (distinguished) economists and (accomplished) engineers alike. On one side stand (impassioned) defenders of the boom, (kindred) spirits of the railway promoters, who treat the opportunity as (sacred) and the doubters as (deranged). On the other stand (seasoned) investors offering an (unimpassioned) reading of the numbers, (dogged) in their skepticism and (unreserved) in their warnings. Most people in between are (engaged) but (distracted), (impressed) by the demonstrations, (acquainted) with the history and (resigned) to riding the wave. The (gnarled) old hands of the trading floor, (henpecked) by risk committees, keep their own counsel. Some (tightfisted) investors, (relieved) to have missed earlier fads, stay on the sidelines; others, (discombobulated) by a market that shrugs off every warning, have grown (dejected).
Is the bulls' optimism (warranted)? Even if AI raises productivity, the gains may be hard to see in official statistics: the (hedonic) adjustments statisticians use to account for better computers struggle with a product whose quality changes monthly. Some of the gloom may prove (unfounded), and some of the hype (unwarranted). Optimism (grounded) in rising profits differs from optimism built on (contrived) metrics, and bulls who argue that price-to-earnings ratios are (outmoded) are repeating a line heard in 1929 and 1999. A (synoptic) view of the past four centuries suggests that the technology usually lives up to the promise while the share prices do not. A (pragmatic) investor might therefore (withhold) judgment on the technology while staying skeptical of the price, which is easier said than done. Optimism lends every prospect a (chromatic) richness; what investors need is an (achromatic) lens, one that corrects for the color a good story adds.
History offers some comfort. Carlota Perez, an economist, argues that technological revolutions typically pass through a speculative “installation” phase, in which financial capital overbuilds the new infrastructure, followed by a crash and then a “deployment” phase in which the technology at last spreads through the economy. Railways and fiber both fit the pattern: the investors were (shattered), but the tracks and cables remained and the economy benefited. If AI follows the same course, today's spending may be (merited) in the long run even if it proves ruinous for those who did the spending, and the (untapped) markets the bulls describe may eventually materialize, if not on their timetable. The appetite for chips will one day be (satiated) and some markets (saturated); the resulting glut, like the fiber glut after 2001, may then be absorbed by uses nobody has yet imagined. The question is not whether a technology is real, since railways and the internet were real, but whether the price is right, and who will bear the losses if it is not.
Every boom is (defined) by the same ingredients: a real innovation, (unbridled) credit, (inflamed) imaginations and warnings (muffled) by the noise of rising prices. The habits are (ingrained). Investors persuade themselves that growth can be (sustained) indefinitely, that today's champions will (wield) their market power forever and (meld) technology and finance into a perpetual-motion machine, and that any firm with a (foothold) in AI will keep it. Each boom claims to break the (mold); lo and (behold), the same assumptions were made about railways, radio and the internet. The (hallowed) names of one boom, from the Railway King to the Nifty Fifty, often end it with reputations (marred) or worse; few emerge (unspotted), and much of the praise turns out to have been (undeserved). Investors' love for a hot stock is often (unrequited), and the (unwonted) caution that follows a crash rarely lasts. There is a (morbid) fascination in reading about the (squalid) ends of (assorted) promoters, from Hudson's flight from his creditors to the (wretched) final years of John Law, yet the (perfervid) boosters and (fervid) believers of each era rarely suppose that they will join the list. The most (collected) investors are usually those who (acquired) their skepticism the hard way, and money (undirected) by any analysis is always the first to flee.
A bubble can behave like a (nova), flaring brightly and then subsiding while the star survives, or like a (supernova), which destroys its star. The railway boom was the first kind; the Mississippi scheme was the second. Which kind AI turns out to be will depend less on the technology than on how much debt is piled on top of it, and on who holds that debt when sentiment turns. Somewhere in an (attic) there are still share certificates from 1720, 1929 and 2000, souvenirs of fortunes that were real until they were not.
A (coda) from the Netherlands. In the hunger winter of 1944-45, under German occupation, starving Dutch families ate tulip bulbs in earnest; the luxury of 1637 had become a famine food. Today the tulip is a national symbol, Delft (ceramic) tulip vases fetch handsome sums at auction, and the flower auction at Aalsmeer is among the largest in the world. The Netherlands still dominates the global trade in flowers and bulbs, a lasting dividend from a craze that Mackay treated as pure folly. Investors' appetite for the next big thing is never (sated) for long, and the whole (panorama) of financial history suggests it never will be. Bubbles are not merely episodes of madness; they are also one way in which societies pay for the future, at a price borne by whoever is holding the asset when the music stops. The trick is not to be that person. The evidence of four centuries is that almost everyone believes they will not be.
translation:
繁花、繁荣与崩盘
从荷兰郁金香到人工智能，四个世纪的投机狂潮，给今天的投资者留下了令人不安的教训
1637年2月的第一周，哈勒姆一家小酒馆里，拍卖人举起一批郁金香球茎，等待一个始终没有出现的出价。短短几天之内，这门被荷兰人戏称为windhandel、即“风中交易”的买卖便陷入停滞；那些以离奇天价订立、用（笔尖/nib）以（潦草难辨的/crabbed）字迹写成的契约，转眼便只值写它们的那张纸了。这一切狂热所追逐的，是从奥斯曼帝国传入的一件（异域/exotic）舶来品——早在它被（栽培/cultivated）于荷兰花园之前，这种花便已是苏丹宫廷中的珍宠。把身家押在这样一样东西上，实在有些古怪。（栀子花/gardenia）浓郁的（香气/aroma）能弥漫满室，大多数郁金香却几乎（毫无香味/unscented）；一个想找点（芬芳馥郁的/aromatic）东西来痴迷的国度，本可以挑得更好。让一株郁金香（声名大噪/celebrated）的是它的模样，尤其是所谓“碎色”品种那（带条纹的/striated）花瓣：白底之上燃着（洋红/magenta）、紫色或深红的火焰纹，宛如手绘。
直到20世纪20年代，植物学家才弄清那些火焰纹从何而来：一种由蚜虫传播的病毒，把色素打散成条纹交错的（马赛克/mosaic），同时耗损了球茎的元气。换言之，最令人垂涎的郁金香其实是病株。它们的美是一种病症；而它们的虚弱——一种植物学意义上的（贫血/anemia）——使其繁殖迟缓，于是供应始终稀缺，价格一路（虚胖膨胀/bloated）。其中最稀有的品种名叫Semper Augustus，意为“永远的奥古斯都”，白底燃着红焰，据说有人为它开出的价钱，足以买下阿姆斯特丹运河边一座（宏伟气派的/majestic）宅邸。约240年后，杰拉德·曼利·霍普金斯将为一切（斑驳的/dappled）事物献上感恩，为那如（毛色斑纹相间的/brindled）母牛般双色交织的天空；而哈勒姆的郁金香迷们早已抢先一步——他们为那些（黑白杂驳的/piebald）、（布满斑点的/maculated）花朵付出了最高的价钱。很难想象还有比这更贴切的泡沫象征：一种资产，其（独特的/characteristic）魅力与一种隐秘的疾病密不可分，人们所倾慕的那种（美感/aesthetic），其成因却无人知晓。
世人对郁金香（狂热/mania）的大部分认知，都来自苏格兰记者查尔斯·麦凯，他的《大癫狂：非同寻常的大众幻想与群众性癫狂》初版于1841年。这本书是一部愚行的（百科全书/encyclopedia），取材（兼收并蓄/eclectic）：炼金术士、算命先生、十字军与鬼屋，同金融泡沫挤在一处；书中的故事如今也已蒙上岁月的（包浆/patina）。麦凯讲到一名水手，把一颗珍贵的球茎错当成洋葱，就着鲱鱼吃了下去——这想必是史上最昂贵的一顿早餐；考虑到郁金香球茎对（胃/gastric）黏膜的刺激，这顿早餐也绝不好受。他还讲到（木讷持重的/stolid）市民倾家荡产，整个国家仿佛（着了魔/possessed）。那位水手的早餐如今已沦为酒馆里的（趣闻谈资/trivia），而其余的许多故事，则属于金融界的（伪经/apocrypha）。此后翻遍荷兰档案的历史学家——尤其是安妮·戈德加——几乎找不到麦凯所描述的那种大规模破产的证据。他所倚重的，主要是崩盘后出版的一批（道德说教式的/moralistic）小册子，其作者怀着（训诫/didactic）之意，又偏爱（煽情夸张的戏码/melodrama）。真实的（传奇/saga）规模更小，也更（平淡无奇/prosaic）：那只是一门（零星断续的/sporadic）买卖，参与者多为商人和殷实的手艺人，对荷兰经济几乎毫发无伤。
然而神话比事实活得更久，因为它有用。每一轮繁荣都需要一则警世寓言，每一个（愤世嫉俗者/cynic）也都需要一根（带刺的讥讽/barb）去掷向多头。麦凯那种（法利赛人式自以为义的/pharisaic）腔调——把贪婪视作别人的毛病——如今看来或许已经（不合时宜/anachronistic）。但他的核心洞见并未过时：用他的话说，人们成群结队地发疯，却只能一个接一个、慢慢地恢复理智。
哈勒姆之后八十三年，这股疯狂越过了北海。1720年，伦敦为南海公司如痴如狂。这家公司此前以承接大笔国债为代价，换得了与西班牙美洲殖民地的贸易垄断权——而这门贸易，西班牙王室一向管得极紧。当年上半年，其股价上涨约八倍，一支由模仿者组成的（无敌舰队/armada）也随之扬帆起航。就连素来（冷静淡漠的/phlegmatic）英国人，也开始（屈服/succumb）于这场热病。在交易巷的咖啡馆里，一个倚着（门框/jamb）的小职员，午饭前就可能发一笔横财；（毫无原则的/unprincipled）发起人四处集资，项目从永动轮到——据传——“一项极为有利可图的事业，但无人知道它是什么”，无所不包。南海公司本身还游说推动了1720年6月的《泡沫法案》，该法试图（禁止/forbid）未获皇家特许的股份公司——与其说是打击投机，不如说是想（保护/shield）自家股价免受对手冲击。
艾萨克·牛顿时任皇家铸币局局长，绝非（缺乏历练的/untutored）投资者。他早早获利了结，却在接近顶点时重新买入，结果损失了一大笔钱，据估算约有两万英镑。他那句（据称/purported）的哀叹——他能算出天体的运行，却算不出人的疯狂——或许只是传说；但亏损是真实的。到年底，南海股票已（吐回/shed）了大部分涨幅。议会调查揭出一条向大臣行贿的（肮脏/sordid）线索，财政大臣被关进了伦敦塔。（痛斥/upbraid）那些一夜暴富的（出身卑贱的/lowbred）股票掮客一时成为风尚，尽管不少公爵也曾加入这场争抢。街头小贩兜售（下流粗俗的/ribald）歪诗，（言辞尖酸的/vinegared）小册子作者把交易巷描绘成一座（堕落的/depraved）贼窝。威廉·贺加斯创作了一幅人物拥挤的（全景式/panoramic）版画，其对时代的（象征意义/emblematic）不逊于那个世纪的任何一幅图像：画中一个（魔鬼般的/diabolic）人物把命运女神剁成碎块，抛向暴民，而各个阶层的市民骑着旋转木马团团打转。
海峡对岸，法国正陷于一场更为离奇的狂热。约翰·劳是一位（四处漂泊的/peripatetic）苏格兰赌徒，过往（劣迹斑斑/checkered）——他曾在伦敦的一场决斗中杀人，又越狱出逃——却凭三寸不烂之舌掌控了法国财政。他的计划带着一股（自大狂/megalomania）的气息：一家发行纸币的国家银行，一家垄断殖民地贸易、吞下国债的独家公司，以及来自路易斯安那的财富许诺——1718年，他的密西西比公司在那条大河沼泽遍布的（三角洲/delta）上建起了新奥尔良。殖民者中有些是被强行押送出海的囚犯，他们成百上千地死于沼泽（恶臭的/fetid）（瘴气/miasma）之中。在巴黎买卖股票的狭窄街道甘康布瓦街上，据说有个驼背人把自己的背租出去当写字台。1720年5月，一纸法令要把股票和钞票的价值减半，民愤之烈，迫使政府不到一周便（撤销/countermand）了这道命令。信心从此再未（恢复/restored），劳在一片骂声中逃离法国。1729年，他在威尼斯穷困而终，葬处离圣马可（广场/piazza）只有几步之遥。
在大众想象中如此（古板持重的/staid）英国维多利亚时代人，其实是（极其活跃的/prolific）投机者。19世纪40年代，他们把积蓄倾注于铁路，议会批准修建数千英里的新线路，其中许多与既有线路重复。“铁路大王”乔治·哈德森被誉为天才，报界把一串溢美之词编成（花环/garland）挂在他的脖子上，直到人们发现，他那（暗箱操作的/underhanded）账目一直在用资本金派发股息。崇拜者纷纷（离弃/deserted）了他，他在国外躲债多年。对投资者而言，这场热潮很难说是一次（彻底的/unqualified）成功；那些从未回本的多余线路上（破败失修的/dilapidated）车站，至今仍散落在英国乡间。然而它也留下了宝贵的遗产：英国铁路网的骨架，由那些再也拿不回本钱的出资人建成。罕见的是，那场热病的（后遗症/sequela）竟是健康的。
同样的几十年里，还出现了“蕨类狂热”——人们迷恋蕨类及其（锯齿状的/serrated）叶片，这个名字由小说家查尔斯·金斯利所起；还有“兰花癫狂”，收藏家们一掷千金购买热带（植物/flora）标本，并派遣（无畏的/intrepid）采集者远赴哥伦比亚和婆罗洲，其中一些人为了一株（兰花/orchid）死于热病。另一些人则迷上了颅相学，它声称能从头皮之下（头颅上的/cephalic）隆起读出人的性格；或是迷上了催眠术，那些（摄人心魄的/hypnotic）表演者场场吸引（座无虚席的/packed）观众。达尔文的表弟弗朗西斯·高尔顿，给世界带来了（优生学的/eugenic）梦想，这一梦想将在随后的世纪里变质为某种（骇人听闻的/horrific）东西。深谙观众心理的吉尔伯特与沙利文写过一部（轻歌剧/operetta），剧中一个南太平洋岛国把自己改组为一家有限责任公司，这样一旦失败，谁也不用掏钱。时至今日，它仍是对公司制度最（滑稽/comic）的诠释，也是最（清晰透彻/pellucid）的诠释之一。
20世纪20年代轮到了美国。收音机是那个时代的奇迹技术，家家屋顶似乎都冒出一根（天线/antenna），美国无线电公司是市场的宠儿。小投资者用保证金买股票，有时只付一成价款；风险最高的股票在一家交易所里买卖，那里的经纪人直到1921年都在露天、在布罗德街的（路边/curb）做生意。操纵股价的投机集团随心所欲地拉抬或打压股价，空头（突袭/raid）是他们惯用的（伎俩/tactic）。在佛罗里达，（潮湿闷热的/humid）沼泽地刚丈量完毕便易手转卖，买家常常连一纸（地契/deed）都没见过，直到1926年一场飓风终结了这股热潮。1929年10月股市崩盘，美国无线电公司开始一路下滑，市值几乎跌得精光。约翰·肯尼思·加尔布雷思所写的大崩盘史至今仍是笔调最（尖刻/acerbic）的一部；他后来又写了一部金融（狂喜/euphoria）简史，书中最归咎的，是金融记忆的短暂：一种集体（失忆/amnesia），让每一代人都得亲自去发现杠杆的乐趣。

（固执己见的/opinionated）评论从不缺乏。电视评论员（装腔作势/histrionic），播客主持人（油嘴滑舌/glib），偶尔有位高管（坦率直言/candid），倒令人耳目一新。（超然无私的/disinterested）观察者——手里没有需要唱多的仓位——实属稀有物种。首席执行官一句（不经意的/unguarded）话，或是大会上一句（即兴/adlib）插话，都能让一只股票的市值涨落数十亿美元。交易大厅里的情绪，一个上午就能从（焦躁不安/agitated）摆到（心满意足/contented），再摆回来；而市场有一种（施虐般的/sadistic）癖好，偏偏在空头认输投降之后反弹，让他们（狼狈难堪/discomfited）。
对于肯留心的人来说，泡沫的迹象就摆在那里。公司在名称或财报电话会上加上“AI”字样，股价便应声跳涨，就像当年“长区块链”那样；2024年，美国监管机构以“AI漂洗”——即夸大对这项技术的使用——为由，对两家投资顾问公司处以罚款，这是对一个（迷恋/infatuated）这一标签的行业所作的早期（训诫/reprimand）。量子计算股——其中许多几乎没有收入——凭借那些必须冷却到（超低温/cryogenic）的机器的前景一飞冲天；大约十年前，一些计划开采（小行星/asteroid）上铂金的（异想天开的/quixotic）初创公司，也曾吸引到大笔真金白银，直到把钱烧光。监管AI是一个（棘手难解的/wicked）问题。为早先时代制定的法律显得（陈旧过时/antiquated），各国政府（三心二意/halfhearted），而那些设立了安全团队的实验室，也有过将其（解散/disband）的先例。一些官员已就规则做过一番（尝试/stab），但一个周期里（姗姗来迟的/belated）改革，往往会遭到下一个周期游说者的抵制。
廉价资金几乎为每一段插曲都添了柴火。维多利亚时代《经济学人》的伟大主编沃尔特·白芝浩——其文笔之（清澈明晰/limpid），至今仍值得一读——曾说，约翰牛能忍受许多事，却忍受不了百分之二的利率：当安全资产收益微薄时，储户就会伸手去够风险更高的资产。漫长的近零利率时代，对投资者的判断力起到了（麻醉剂/anesthetic）的作用。不断上涨的价格是一种强效的（镇痛/analgesia），能麻痹怀疑带来的痛楚；而当价格不再上涨时，市场最爱的（止痛药/analgesic）就是降息。宽松信贷是一种（麻醉品/narcotic）；自1987年以来，几乎每逢市场一晃动，央行便打上一（针/hypodermic）流动性，让市场学会了期待下一针。美联储前主席威廉·麦克切斯尼·马丁说过，央行的职责是在派对刚热闹起来时撤走潘趣酒碗；而一个患上（嗜酒狂/dipsomania）的市场，从不会为此心存感激。今天的央行行长们，职业要求他们（心平气和/even-tempered），言辞也（字斟句酌/measured），但他们有充分的理由（失眠/insomnia）。他们（循序渐进的/graduated）加息与降息方式，过去曾（抑制/damped）了波动，却无法废除周期。
好时光里（流动性充裕的/liquid）市场，到了坏时光就会变得（黏滞/viscid）：买家恰恰在卖家最需要他们的时候消失不见。一个（平静无波/placid）、甚至（慵懒倦怠/languid）的夏天，可能让位于一个（忙乱不堪/hectic）的秋季交易期；一波（炽热的/torrid）上涨行情，也可能换来每一次新股发行都遭（冷遇/frigid）。估值模型假设世界是（静止的/static），但运动中的市场所蕴含的（动能/kinetic）难以遏止；而当它反转时，反弹变得（时断时续/spasmodic），成交（冷淡/tepid），价格（低迷/depressed），情绪（消沉/subdued）。过度自信在基金经理中是（慢性/chronic）通病，（暴躁易怒的/choleric）交易员调养着（消化性/peptic）溃疡，而一位曾被众星捧月的创始人向债主苦苦哀求的场面，既（可怜可悲/pathetic），又似曾相识。AI支出若（明显/marked）放缓，将给依赖它的供应商造成（严重破坏/havoc）；一个过于（僵化/rigid）而无法适应的商业模式将难以存活；就连客户对一款新模型反应（平淡/muted），也可能造成损害。
那么，一位（头脑冷静的/levelheaded）投资者该何去何从？这个（两难困境/dilemma）由来已久。泡沫很少是（蓄谋已久的/premeditated）阴谋；它们是（未经预谋的/unpremeditated）集体行为，数以百万计（衣冠楚楚/well-groomed）、（消息灵通/informed）、在别的事情上也（精明务实/hardheaded）的人们彼此说服。经历过2000年和2008年、（饱经风霜/wizened）的老手们，以（猜疑挑剔/jaundiced）的眼光看待这轮繁荣；年轻的交易员们则（迷恋/enamored）这项技术，又早已（习惯了/inured）那些似乎总会被央行扭转的回撤，因而（不为所动/unmoved）。两个阵营都可能（故步自封/closed-minded）。20世纪90年代末那些（脾气乖戾的/dyspeptic）空头最终是对的，但他们（时机错判的/mistimed）押注在此期间让他们付出了惨重代价；一句通常被归于凯恩斯名下的话——市场保持非理性的时间，可能比你保持偿付能力的时间更长——道出了这一点，尽管这句话的出处本身也（缺乏依据/unsubstantiated）。就连（意兴阑珊、见怪不怪的/jaded）分析师也承认，爬到（树枝/limb）末梢去孤身对抗一个（羽翼丰满的/full-fledged）泡沫，不是（胆小怯懦/fainthearted）者干得了的；而眼下，（胆大无畏的/stouthearted）多头在这场争论中占了上风。
这场争论让（卓有声望的/distinguished）经济学家和（成就斐然的/accomplished）工程师同样分成两派。一边是这轮繁荣（慷慨激昂的/impassioned）捍卫者，他们与当年的铁路发起人（气味相投/kindred），视这一机遇为（神圣/sacred），视怀疑者为（疯癫/deranged）。另一边是（老练的/seasoned）投资者，他们对数字作出（冷静客观的/unimpassioned）解读，在怀疑上（锲而不舍/dogged），在警告上（毫无保留/unreserved）。夹在中间的大多数人，既（投入其中/engaged）又（心不在焉/distracted），为种种演示所（折服/impressed），对历史也（有所了解/acquainted），却（无可奈何地/resigned）随波逐流。交易大厅里那些（骨节嶙峋、饱经沧桑的/gnarled）老手，被风控委员会（管得服服帖帖/henpecked），对自己的看法守口如瓶。一些（吝啬抠门的/tightfisted）投资者，（庆幸/relieved）自己错过了早先的几轮热潮，依旧作壁上观；另一些人则被一个对一切警告都置若罔闻的市场弄得（晕头转向/discombobulated），日渐（垂头丧气/dejected）。
多头的乐观是否（有道理/warranted）？即便AI提高了生产率，这些收益也可能难以在官方统计中显现：统计学家用来反映计算机性能改进的（享乐/hedonic）价格调整，面对一种质量每月都在变化的产品时力不从心。有些悲观或许会被证明（毫无根据/unfounded），有些炒作则（缺乏正当理由/unwarranted）。（立足于/grounded）利润增长的乐观，有别于建立在（人为拼凑的/contrived）指标之上的乐观；那些声称市盈率已经（过时/outmoded）的多头，不过是在重复1929年和1999年就听过的论调。对过去四个世纪的（概览式/synoptic）审视表明，技术通常会兑现承诺，股价却不会。因此，一位（务实的/pragmatic）投资者或许会对技术（暂缓/withhold）下判断，同时对价格保持怀疑——这说来容易做来难。乐观会为每一种前景添上（斑斓多彩/chromatic）的丰富色调；投资者需要的，是一片（消色差的/achromatic）透镜，用来校正一个好故事额外添加的色彩。
历史也提供了些许慰藉。经济学家卡萝塔·佩蕾丝认为，技术革命通常要经历一个投机性的“导入期”——金融资本过度建设新的基础设施——随后是一场崩盘，然后才进入“展开期”，技术终于在整个经济中扩散开来。铁路和光纤都符合这一模式：投资者（心碎梦断/shattered），但铁轨和光缆留了下来，经济从中受益。如果AI也走上同样的道路，那么从长远看，今天的支出或许是（值得的/merited），即便它对花钱的人来说是毁灭性的；多头所描绘的那些（尚未开发的/untapped）市场，终有一天或许会成为现实，只是未必按他们的时间表。对芯片的胃口总有一天会被（喂饱/satiated），一些市场也会（饱和/saturated）；由此产生的过剩，就像2001年之后的光纤过剩一样，届时或许会被如今谁也想象不到的用途所吸收。问题不在于一项技术是否真实——铁路和互联网都是真实的——而在于价格是否合理，以及万一不合理，谁来承担损失。
每一轮繁荣都由同样的成分所（界定/defined）：一项真实的创新，（毫无节制的/unbridled）信贷，被（点燃/inflamed）的想象力，以及被价格上涨的喧嚣所（掩盖/muffled）的警告。这些习性（根深蒂固/ingrained）。投资者说服自己：增长可以无限（持续/sustained）；今天的冠军将永远（挥舞/wield）其市场权力，并把技术与金融（熔合/meld）成一台永动机；任何在AI领域站稳（脚跟/foothold）的公司都将守住阵地。每一轮繁荣都宣称自己打破了（旧模子/mold）；可是（瞧/behold），同样的假设当年也曾用在铁路、无线电和互联网身上。一轮繁荣中那些（被奉若神明的/hallowed）名字，从“铁路大王”到“漂亮五十”，往往以声誉（受损/marred）乃至更糟的结局收场；鲜有人能（清白无瑕/unspotted）地全身而退，许多赞誉事后证明（名不副实/undeserved）。投资者对一只热门股的爱常常是（单相思/unrequited），而崩盘之后那种（反常的/unwonted）谨慎很少能持久。阅读（形形色色的/assorted）发起人那些（不堪的/squalid）下场——从哈德森躲债出逃，到约翰·劳（凄惨的/wretched）晚年——有一种（病态的/morbid）吸引力；然而每个时代（狂热至极的/perfervid）鼓吹者和（热忱的/fervid）信徒，很少会想到自己也会被列入这份名单。最（沉着镇定的/collected）投资者，通常是那些吃尽苦头才（习得/acquired）怀疑精神的人；而（不受任何分析指引的/undirected）钱，总是最先逃离。
泡沫的表现可以像一颗（新星/nova）：骤然大放光芒，随后归于黯淡，而恒星本身得以幸存；也可以像一颗（超新星/supernova），把自己的恒星彻底摧毁。铁路热属于前一种，密西西比计划属于后一种。AI究竟属于哪一种，与其说取决于技术，不如说取决于堆在它上面的债务有多少，以及市场情绪逆转时，这些债务握在谁的手里。在某个（阁楼/attic）里，至今仍存放着1720年、1929年和2000年的股票凭证——它们是一笔笔财富的纪念品，那些财富曾经真实，直到不再真实。
最后，是来自荷兰的一段（尾声/coda）。1944至1945年的“饥饿之冬”，在德国占领下，饥肠辘辘的荷兰家庭真的吃起了郁金香球茎；1637年的奢侈品，变成了饥荒时的口粮。如今，郁金香是荷兰的国家象征，代尔夫特的（陶瓷/ceramic）郁金香花瓶在拍卖会上能卖出可观的高价，阿尔斯梅尔的鲜花拍卖市场跻身世界最大之列。荷兰至今仍主导着全球鲜花和球茎贸易——这是一场被麦凯视为纯粹愚行的狂热所留下的长久红利。投资者对下一个大热门的胃口从不会长久地得到（满足/sated），而整幅金融史的（全景/panorama）表明，它永远也不会。泡沫不仅仅是一段段疯狂的插曲；它们也是社会为未来买单的一种方式，代价由音乐停止时手里还握着资产的人承担。诀窍在于，别做那个人。四个世纪的证据表明，几乎每个人都相信自己不会是那个人。
text:
本批词根亮点：

• utopia：ou（无）+ topos（地方），不存在的地方=乌托邦，托马斯·莫尔1516年创造，dystopia（反乌托邦）是其对应词

• cornucopia：cornu（角）+ copia（丰富），希腊神话中阿玛尔西亚的丰饶角，copy（拷贝）和 copious（丰富的）同根

• trivia：古罗马十字路口（tri+via=三条路）公告板上张贴的无关紧要信息，trivial（琐碎的）由此而来

• chimera：希腊神话中狮头羊身蛇尾怪兽，引申为不可能实现的幻想

• magenta：以1859年法国在意大利北部马真塔镇击败奥地利军队命名的品红色染料

• snob：18世纪剑桥俚语指非贵族出身的学生（shoe + nob），后演变为自视高人一等的人

• aplomb：法语“铅锤般垂直”（à plomb），像铅锤一样沉稳=沉着，plumber（水管工）同根

• larva：拉丁语“幽灵/面具”，因幼虫外形隐藏了成虫面貌而得名

quiz.question: _____ replica
quiz.explanation: 复制品，精确的复制品。The museum displayed an exact replica of the ancient artifact. 博物馆展出了古代文物的精确的复制品。 | replic->折回（拉丁replicare->折叠回），replica->折回原样的复制品（cf. reply回复=折回，replicate复制，application申请） || 文化联想：景区里按原尺寸复刻的一尊兵马俑可以用 replica 来称呼，它不是原物，而是尽量把原物外形完整复制出来的“复制品”，可以说 **a Terracotta Warrior replica — “The museum displayed a life-size Terracotta Warrior replica modeled on the famous figures from Xi'an.”**

quiz.question: _______ armada
quiz.explanation: 舰队，西班牙舰队。The Spanish armada sailed against England in 1588. 西班牙舰队在1588年向英格兰进发。 | armar->武装（西班牙语，拉丁armare），armada->武装的船队=舰队（cf. arm手臂/武装，armor盔甲，army军队） || 文化联想：郑和下西洋时数百艘宝船、战船与补给船浩浩荡荡出海的庞大船队，可以用 armada 来形容；armada 强调的正是规模庞大、气势惊人的舰队，可以说 **Zheng He's armada — “Zheng He's armada sailed across the Indian Ocean during the Ming dynasty.”**

quiz.question: _______ agenda
quiz.explanation: 议程，会议议程。The secretary prepared the meeting agenda for discussion. 秘书准备了讨论的会议议程。 | agend->需要被做的事（拉丁agere->做），agenda->待办事项的清单（cf. act行动，agent代理人，agile敏捷，cf. agenda复数=多件事） || 文化联想：“两会”召开前公布的一项项审议、讨论和表决事项，就是 agenda 所表达的“要处理的事项清单”，可以说 **the Two Sessions agenda — “The Two Sessions agenda lists the major proposals, debates, and votes to be handled during the meetings.”**

quiz.question: _____ coda
quiz.explanation: 尾声，音乐尾声。The symphony ended with a beautiful music coda. 交响乐以美妙的音乐尾声结束。 | coda->尾巴（意大利语，拉丁cauda），coda->音乐的收尾段（cf. codicil遗嘱附录，queue队列=尾巴，cauda尾巴） || 文化联想：一部大型民乐作品在最后重新收束主题、把全曲稳稳落下的尾声，可以用 coda 来称呼；coda 就是作品结尾的收束段，可以说 **the coda of a Chinese orchestral piece — “The Chinese orchestral piece ended with a coda that brought its main theme back one last time.”**

quiz.question: _________ panacea
quiz.explanation: 万能药，万能的万能药。There is no universal panacea for all of life's problems. 没有万能的万能药能解决生活中的所有问题。 | pan->全部（希腊），acea->治愈（希腊akos），panacea->治愈所有的=万能药（cf. pandemic全球流行，panorama全景，pantheism泛神论） || 文化联想：江湖郎中号称一颗“大力丸”能包治百病，这种被吹成什么问题都能解决的万能药，正是 panacea 最典型的形象，可以说 **a panacea — “A quack doctor might advertise a so-called magic pill as a panacea for every illness.”**

quiz.question: ______ saga
quiz.explanation: 传奇故事，家族传奇故事。The novel told a long family saga spanning generations. 这部小说讲述了一个跨越几代人的漫长家族传奇故事。 | saga->故事（古挪威，sagas北欧英雄传说），saga->长篇历史传奇（cf. sage智者，say说，cf. Norse sagas冰岛传说） || 文化联想：《三国演义》从群雄并起写到三国归晋，人物和兴亡跨越数十年，这种篇幅宏大、延续多代事件的传奇叙事很适合用 saga 来形容，可以说 **the Three Kingdoms saga — “Romance of the Three Kingdoms unfolds as a sprawling historical saga of war, ambition, and dynastic change.”**

quiz.question: ________ apocrypha
quiz.explanation: 伪经，圣经伪经。Scholars debate the authenticity of biblical apocrypha. 学者们争论圣经伪经的真实性。 | apo->离开，krypt->隐藏（希腊），apocrypha->隐藏起来的书=伪经（cf. crypt地下室，cryptic神秘，encryption加密） || 文化联想：正史之外流传的帝王秘闻、宫廷逸事和真假难辨的野史，很适合让人联想到 apocrypha；它指的正是未被正统经典承认、却在民间流传的材料，可以说 **historical apocrypha — “Many sensational palace stories survived only as historical apocrypha rather than accepted official history.”**

quiz.question: ______ phobia
quiz.explanation: 恐惧症，社交恐惧症。She struggled with social phobia in crowded places. 她在拥挤的地方与社交恐惧症作斗争。 | phob->恐惧（希腊phobos），phobia->非理性的强烈恐惧（cf. claustrophobia幽闭恐惧，acrophobia恐高，xenophobia仇外） || 文化联想：中文网络里常说的“密集恐惧症”“幽闭恐惧症”中的“恐惧症”，核心概念就是 phobia：对某类对象产生强烈、往往不合比例的恐惧，可以说 **a phobia — “An extreme and irrational fear of tightly packed holes is a phobia often discussed online in China.”**

quiz.question: ____ acrophobia
quiz.explanation: 恐高症，患有恐高症。People who have acrophobia fear heights intensely. 患有恐高症的人非常害怕高度。 | acro->顶端（希腊akros），phobia->恐惧，acrophobia->对高处的恐惧（cf. acrobat杂技=高处走，acropolis雅典卫城，acronym首字母词） || 文化联想：站上华山长空栈道往脚下悬崖一看就腿软、心慌、不敢再往前，这种对高处的强烈恐惧就是 acrophobia，可以说 **acrophobia on the Huashan plank walk — “A tourist with acrophobia may find it terrifying to look down from the Huashan plank walk.”**

quiz.question: fascia _____
quiz.explanation: 筋膜板，筋膜板。The carpenter installed the fascia board under the roof edge. 木匠在屋顶边缘下安装了筋膜板。 | fascia->束/带（拉丁，fasces->捆束），fascia->成束的结缔组织/带状板（cf. fascism法西斯=束棒符号，fascinate迷住=束缚） || 文化联想：如今国内健身房里常说“筋膜枪放松筋膜”，这里的“筋膜”就是 fascia：包裹、连接肌肉等组织的一层结缔组织，可以说 **muscle fascia — “A massage gun is often used to relax tight muscle fascia after exercise.”**

quiz.question: ______ encyclopedia
quiz.explanation: 百科全书，袖珍百科全书。She carried a pocket encyclopedia for quick reference. 她随身携带袖珍百科全书以便快速查阅。 | enkyklios->圆形/普遍（希腊），paideia->教育，encyclopedia->圆形教育=百科全书（cf. cycle循环，pedagogy教育学，pedant学究） || 文化联想：《永乐大典》试图把天下典籍与知识汇聚一处，这种囊括众多学科、供人查考的知识总汇最容易让人联想到 encyclopedia，可以说 **an encyclopedia of Chinese learning — “The Yongle Encyclopedia was conceived as an encyclopedia of Chinese learning on an extraordinary scale.”**

quiz.question: _____ nostalgia
quiz.explanation: 怀旧，甜蜜的怀旧。He felt sweet nostalgia when visiting his childhood home. 他访问童年住所时感到甜蜜的怀旧。 | nostos->归家（希腊），algia->痛（希腊），nostalgia->想回家的痛=怀旧（cf. algae海藻，nostalgia最初指士兵想家的病症） || 文化联想：回到拆迁前住过的老胡同，看到搪瓷缸、旧收音机和儿时小卖部而突然想起过去，那种对旧日时光又甜又酸的眷恋就是 nostalgia，可以说 **nostalgia for the old hutong — “Walking through an old Beijing hutong can awaken deep nostalgia for a vanished way of life.”**

quiz.question: hemophilia _______
quiz.explanation: 血友病，血友病携带者。She was a hemophilia carrier but showed no symptoms. 她是血友病携带者，但没有表现出症状。 | hemo->血（希腊haima），philia->喜爱/倾向，hemophilia->血液倾向流不止=血友病（cf. hemoglobin血红蛋白，hemostasis止血） || 文化联想：中国医院血液科里，有些患者因为遗传性凝血因子缺乏而一旦出血就很难止住，这种疾病就是 hemophilia，可以说 **hemophilia — “A patient with hemophilia may bleed for a long time after even a small injury.”**

quiz.question: ____-__________ anemia
quiz.explanation: 贫血，缺铁性贫血。The doctor diagnosed iron-deficiency anemia and prescribed supplements. 医生诊断为缺铁性贫血并开了补充剂。 | an->无，emia->血（希腊haima），anemia->血液不足=贫血（cf. hemoglobin血红蛋白，leukemia白血病，anemic贫血的） || 文化联想：一个人长期脸色苍白、容易乏力，验血发现血红蛋白明显偏低，这在中文里说“贫血”，英文就是 anemia，可以说 **anemia — “Persistent fatigue and a pale complexion may lead a doctor to test a patient for anemia.”**

quiz.question: ________ mania
quiz.explanation: 狂热，足球狂热。During the World Cup, football mania swept the nation. 世界杯期间，足球狂热席卷全国。 | mania->疯狂（希腊mainesthai->疯），mania->狂热/强迫症（cf. maniac疯子，manic狂躁，dementia痴呆） || 文化联想：上世纪八九十年代一度席卷全国的“气功热”，很多人近乎狂热地追逐各种功法和大师，这种社会性的狂热状态很容易让人联想到 mania，可以说 **qigong mania — “During the qigong boom of the 1980s and 1990s, qigong mania swept through many Chinese cities.”**

quiz.question: _________ megalomania
quiz.explanation: 自大狂，政治自大狂。The dictator's political megalomania knew no bounds. 独裁者的政治自大狂没有界限。 | megalo->巨大（希腊megas），mania->狂，megalomania->关于伟大的狂热=自大狂（cf. megalopolis超大城市，megaphone扩音器，mega巨大） || 文化联想：古代帝王若自认功业前无古人、执意兴建巨型宫殿和纪功工程来证明自己“伟大无边”，这种极端自我膨胀很适合用 megalomania 来形容，可以说 **imperial megalomania — “An emperor obsessed with gigantic monuments and his own greatness may display imperial megalomania.”**

quiz.question: monomania ___ _____
quiz.explanation: 偏执狂，对秩序的偏执狂。His monomania for order made him organize everything obsessively. 他对秩序的偏执狂让他强迫性地整理一切。 | mono->单一（希腊），mania->狂，monomania->对单一事物的狂热=偏执（cf. monopoly垄断，monologue独白，monotony单调） || 文化联想：《儒林外史》里范进大半生几乎只剩“中举”这一个念头，这种被单一目标占据全部心思的偏执迷恋，很容易让人联想到 monomania，可以说 **Fan Jin's monomania — “Fan Jin's monomania for passing the imperial examination consumed nearly every part of his life.”**

quiz.question: pyromania ____
quiz.explanation: 纵火狂，纵火狂案例。The psychiatrist studied the pyromania case carefully. 精神病医生仔细研究了纵火狂案例。 | pyro->火（希腊pyr），mania->狂，pyromania->对火的强迫性狂热=纵火狂（cf. pyrotechnics烟火技术，pyre火葬堆，pyrex耐热玻璃） || 文化联想：如果一个人并非为了报复或获利，而是反复产生难以控制的纵火冲动、看到火焰就异常兴奋，这种病理性的纵火冲动才是 pyromania，可以说 **pyromania — “Repeated urges to set fires for the thrill of it are characteristic of pyromania.”**

quiz.question: _______ dipsomania
quiz.explanation: 酗酒狂，酒精酗酒狂。His alcohol dipsomania required professional treatment. 他的酒精酗酒狂需要专业治疗。 | dipso->口渴（希腊dipsa），mania->狂，dipsomania->对饮酒的狂热渴望=酗酒狂（cf. dipsomaniac酗酒狂，thirst渴，dipsomania=病理性饮酒冲动） || 文化联想：中国文学里常有“嗜酒如命”的酒徒形象；若这种饮酒欲望发展成难以自控、反复发作的强迫性冲动，就很接近 dipsomania 的本义，可以说 **dipsomania — “A fictional drinker who cannot resist repeated bouts of heavy drinking may be described as suffering from dipsomania.”**

quiz.question: gardenia _______
quiz.explanation: 栀子花，栀子花花朵。The fragrant gardenia blossom filled the garden with perfume. 芳香的栀子花花朵让花园充满香气。 | Gardenia->以苏格兰植物学家亚历山大·加登命名，gardenia->栀子花（cf. garden花园，cf. 以人名命名的植物） || 文化联想：江南初夏白色栀子花开时，院子里常能闻到浓烈清甜的香气，过去也有人把花别在发间；这种白花本身就是 gardenia，可以说 **a gardenia — “A white gardenia tucked into the hair was once a familiar summer sight in parts of southern China.”**

quiz.question: ________ insignia
quiz.explanation: 徽章，军事徽章。The officer wore military insignia on his uniform. 军官在制服上佩戴军事徽章。 | in->上面，sign->标记（拉丁signum），insignia->标记在上的=徽章（cf. sign标志，signal信号，signature签名，insignificant微不足道） || 文化联想：解放军军帽或军徽上的“八一”标志，用来表明身份和所属组织，这种正式的徽记就是 insignia，可以说 **the August First insignia — “The August First insignia immediately identifies the military tradition associated with the People's Liberation Army.”**

quiz.question: ______ insomnia
quiz.explanation: 失眠，遭受失眠。Many people suffer insomnia due to stress. 许多人因压力而遭受失眠。 | in->否定，somn->睡眠（拉丁somnus），insomnia->无法睡眠（cf. dormitory宿舍，somnambulism梦游，somnolent困倦，dormant休眠） || 文化联想：古诗词里常写“夜不能寐”、独坐听更漏直到天明，那种明明想睡却久久无法入睡的状态就是 insomnia，可以说 **a night of insomnia — “A poet listening to the night watch until dawn might be enduring a night of insomnia.”**

quiz.question: paranoia ________
quiz.explanation: 偏执症，偏执症障碍。The patient was diagnosed with paranoia disorder. 患者被诊断患有偏执症障碍。 | para->旁边/反常（希腊），noia->心智（希腊nous），paranoia->偏离正常心智=偏执症（cf. paranoid偏执的，paranormal超自然） || 文化联想：清代文字狱中，统治者从诗句、字眼里反复猜疑作者是否暗藏谋逆之意，这种处处怀疑有人加害或阴谋针对自己的心理，很容易让人联想到 paranoia，可以说 **paranoia — “The suspicion surrounding literary inquisitions can be understood as a form of political paranoia.”**

quiz.question: cornucopia __ _______
quiz.explanation: 丰饶，选择的丰饶。The buffet offered a cornucopia of options for diners. 自助餐为食客提供了选择的丰饶。 | cornu->角（拉丁），copia->丰富，cornucopia->丰饶角（希腊神话中阿玛尔西亚的角，cf. copy拷贝，copious丰富） || 文化联想：春节年夜饭一桌十几二十道菜，鸡鸭鱼肉、点心水果摆得满满当当，这种“丰盛得像取之不尽”的景象很适合用 cornucopia 来形容，可以说 **a cornucopia of New Year dishes — “A lavish New Year's Eve banquet can look like a cornucopia of festive dishes.”**

quiz.question: _____ utopia
quiz.explanation: 乌托邦，理想的乌托邦。The philosopher described his vision of an ideal utopia. 哲学家描述了他对理想的乌托邦的愿景。 | u->无（希腊ou），topia->地方（希腊topos），utopia->不存在的地方=乌托邦（托马斯·莫尔1516年创造，cf. dystopia反乌托邦） || 文化联想：陶渊明《桃花源记》里与世隔绝、安宁自足的桃花源，是中国文化中最典型的理想世界想象，也正好对应 utopia，可以说 **the Peach Blossom utopia — “Tao Yuanming's Peach Blossom Spring has long served as a Chinese image of utopia.”**

quiz.question: _________ myopia
quiz.explanation: 短视，营销短视。The company suffered from marketing myopia and lost customers. 公司遭受营销短视并失去了客户。 | myo->闭合（希腊myein->闭眼），opia->视力（希腊），myopia->眯眼看=近视/短视（cf. myopic短视的，hyperopia远视，telescope望远镜） || 文化联想：“杀鸡取卵”只顾眼前得到鸡蛋，却毁掉以后持续产蛋的可能，这种看得到近利、看不到长远后果的短视正是 myopia 的比喻义，可以说 **economic myopia — “Selling tomorrow's future for today's gain is a classic example of economic myopia.”**

quiz.question: _____ aria
quiz.explanation: 咏叹调，歌剧咏叹调。The soprano sang a beautiful opera aria. 女高音唱了一首美妙的歌剧咏叹调。 | aria->咏唱（意大利语，拉丁aer->空气），aria->歌剧中的独唱曲（cf. air旋律/空气，airy轻盈，aura氛围） || 文化联想：京剧里主角暂时停下对白，用一大段独唱唱腔集中抒发情绪；虽然体裁不同，但这种“独唱承担情感核心”的功能很容易帮助理解 aria，可以说 **an aria-like solo passage — “A long solo passage in Peking opera can function rather like an aria by concentrating a character's emotion in song.”**

quiz.question: _______ bacteria
quiz.explanation: 细菌，有害的细菌。Washing hands removes harmful bacteria. 洗手可以去除有害的细菌。 | bakterion->小棒（希腊，因早期显微镜下杆状），bacteria->杆状微生物=细菌（cf. bacterium单数，antibiotic抗生素，probiotic益生菌） || 文化联想：四川泡菜坛能发酸发香，关键参与者之一就是乳酸菌；这些肉眼看不见的微生物都属于 bacteria，可以说 **lactic-acid bacteria — “Lactic-acid bacteria help give traditional Chinese pickles their sour flavor.”**

quiz.question: ____ __ euphoria
quiz.explanation: 欣快感，欣快感的浪潮。The victory brought a wave of euphoria to the fans. 胜利给球迷带来了欣快感的浪潮。 | eu->好（希腊），phor->携带（希腊pherein），euphoria->承载着好的感觉=欣快感（cf. euphemism委婉，euphony悦耳，dysphoria烦躁） || 文化联想：2001年北京申奥成功的消息宣布后，人群在街头彻夜欢呼，那种短时间内席卷许多人的强烈兴奋和狂喜，可以用 euphoria 来形容，可以说 **public euphoria — “Beijing's successful 2001 Olympic bid triggered public euphoria across the country.”**

quiz.question: __________ fantasia
quiz.explanation: 幻想曲，管弦乐幻想曲。The composer wrote an elaborate orchestral fantasia. 作曲家创作了一首精心制作的管弦乐幻想曲。 | phantasia->显现（希腊phainein->显示），fantasia->想象中显现的=幻想曲（cf. phantom幻影，fantasy幻想，fantasy=fantasia的英语形式） || 文化联想：把《茉莉花》的旋律拿来自由变奏、忽快忽慢、不断展开想象式改编，这种不拘固定曲式的幻想性器乐创作很适合称为 fantasia，可以说 **a fantasia on 'Jasmine Flower' — “A composer could turn the melody of 'Jasmine Flower' into a free-form fantasia.”**

quiz.question: _____ analgesia
quiz.explanation: 镇痛，局部镇痛。The dentist applied local analgesia before the procedure. 牙医在手术前进行了局部镇痛。 | an->无，alg->痛（希腊algos），analgesia->无痛状态=镇痛（cf. analgesic镇痛药，nostalgia怀旧=想家的痛，neuralgia神经痛） || 文化联想：中国语境里常说“针灸镇痛”，其中“疼痛被减轻或消失的状态”就是 analgesia 所表达的核心概念，可以说 **acupuncture analgesia — “Modern studies have examined acupuncture analgesia as a way of reducing pain.”**

quiz.question: _________ amnesia
quiz.explanation: 失忆症，暂时性失忆症。After the accident, he suffered temporary amnesia. 事故后，他患上了暂时性失忆症。 | a->无，mnesia->记忆（希腊mneme），amnesia->无记忆=失忆症（cf. mnemonic记忆术，amnesty特赦=忘记罪行，Mnemosyne记忆女神） || 文化联想：武侠和电视剧里常见人物受伤醒来后把姓名、身世和旧事全忘了，这种“记忆缺失”的经典桥段就是 amnesia，可以说 **amnesia — “A wuxia hero who wakes after an injury with no memory of his past is suffering from amnesia.”**

quiz.question: _____ militia
quiz.explanation: 民兵，地方民兵。The local militia defended the village. 地方民兵保卫了村庄。 | miles->士兵（拉丁），militia->公民兵役组织=民兵（cf. military军事，militant好战的，militate对抗，mile英里=千步） || 文化联想：抗战题材里的村民平时种地、遇到敌情就组织起来站岗、埋地雷、保卫村庄，这类非职业军人的地方武装就是 militia，可以说 **village militia — “A village militia could farm in peacetime and organize local defense when danger arrived.”**

quiz.question: _________ inertia
quiz.explanation: 惯性，牛顿惯性。Physics students study Newtonian inertia. 物理学生学习牛顿惯性。 | iners->无技能/懒（拉丁，in+ars->无技艺），inertia->无活动性=惯性（cf. inert惰性，art艺术，artisan工匠，inertia牛顿第一定律） || 文化联想：一个单位明知旧制度效率低，却因为“以前一直这么办”而迟迟不愿改变，这种靠原有状态自己延续下去的惰性正是 inertia 的比喻义，可以说 **institutional inertia — “The phrase 'we have always done it this way' is a perfect expression of institutional inertia.”**

quiz.question: _______ minutia
quiz.explanation: 细节，琐碎的细节。Don't get lost in trivial minutia; focus on the big picture. 不要迷失在琐碎的细节中；关注大局。 | minut->细小（拉丁minutus），minutia->极小的细节（cf. minute分钟/细小，mini迷你，diminish减少，miniature小型） || 文化联想：中文说“鸡毛蒜皮”，就是那些小到几乎不影响大局却被反复计较的细枝末节，这正是 minutia，可以说 **the minutia of daily life — “Arguments over tiny household details can become arguments over the minutia of daily life.”**

quiz.question: _______ trivia
quiz.explanation: 琐事，无用的琐事。His head was full of useless trivia. 他的脑子里充满了无用的琐事。 | tri->三，via->路（拉丁），trivia->三叉路口=琐碎信息（古罗马三叉路口公告板上贴无关紧要信息，cf. trivial琐碎，via经由） || 文化联想：饭桌上有人专门讲“乾隆到底吃什么”“某个汉字最早怎么写”之类无关大局却有趣的冷知识，这些零碎小知识就是 trivia，可以说 **Chinese-history trivia — “A dinner-table conversation about obscure facts from Chinese history can turn into Chinese-history trivia.”**

quiz.question: dyslexia _________
quiz.explanation: 阅读障碍，阅读障碍诊断。Early dyslexia diagnosis can help with treatment. 早期阅读障碍诊断可以帮助治疗。 | dys->困难（希腊），lexia->阅读（希腊lexis->词），dyslexia->阅读困难=阅读障碍（cf. dysfunctional失调，lexicon词汇，lexis词汇） || 文化联想：一个孩子智力和视力都正常，却长期在识字、拼读和阅读流畅度上异常困难，在中文课堂里这种阅读障碍就可以用 dyslexia 来称呼，可以说 **dyslexia — “A child with dyslexia may have persistent difficulty reading characters despite normal intelligence and vision.”**

quiz.question: anorexia _______
quiz.explanation: 厌食症，神经性厌食症。She received treatment for anorexia nervosa. 她接受了神经性厌食症的治疗。 | an->无，orexia->食欲（希腊orexis），anorexia->无食欲=厌食症（cf. anorectic厌食的，bulimia暴食症，appetite食欲） || 文化联想：中文里说一个人大病之后“完全没胃口、什么都吃不下”，这种明显缺乏食欲的状态在医学英语里可以用 anorexia 表示，可以说 **anorexia — “After a serious illness, a patient with severe loss of appetite may be described medically as having anorexia.”**

quiz.question: asphyxia _____
quiz.explanation: 窒息，窒息死亡。The autopsy revealed asphyxia death as the cause. 尸检显示窒息死亡是死因。 | a->无，sphyxia->脉搏（希腊sphyxis），asphyxia->脉搏停止=窒息（cf. asphyxiate使窒息，suffocate窒息，pulse脉搏） || 文化联想：过去冬天门窗紧闭烧蜂窝煤，如果一氧化碳积聚，人会因缺氧而失去意识甚至死亡；这种窒息状态就是 asphyxia，可以说 **asphyxia — “Burning coal in a sealed room can cause carbon-monoxide poisoning and fatal asphyxia.”**

quiz.question: ___-_____ parka
quiz.explanation: 派克大衣，毛皮内衬派克大衣。She wore a warm fur-lined parka in the Arctic. 她在北极穿着温暖的毛皮内衬派克大衣。 | parka->毛皮上衣（涅涅茨语，西伯利亚土著），parka->原为因纽特人的毛皮外套（cf. anorak风衣=格陵兰因纽特语） || 文化联想：东北严冬里常见那种带帽、厚实、能把上半身严严实实裹住的防寒外套，外形和用途都很接近 parka，可以说 **a winter parka — “A thick hooded winter parka is practical clothing for the bitter cold of northeast China.”**

quiz.question: _______ sequela
quiz.explanation: 后遗症，疾病后遗症。The disease sequela affected him for years. 疾病后遗症影响了他多年。 | sequ->跟随（拉丁sequi），sequela->疾病之后跟随的=后遗症（cf. sequel续集，sequence序列，consequence后果，subsequent随后） || 文化联想：一个人脑卒中抢救成功后仍长期留下偏瘫、语言障碍等问题，这种原发疾病过去之后继续存在的后果就是 sequela，可以说 **a neurological sequela — “Weakness on one side of the body after a stroke may remain as a neurological sequela.”**

quiz.question: ________ gorilla
quiz.explanation: 大猩猩，山地大猩猩。The mountain gorilla is an endangered species. 山地大猩猩是濒危物种。 | gorilla->野蛮毛人（希腊Gorillai，北非土著词），gorilla->大猩猩（汉诺的航海记中记载，cf. guerrilla游击队=小型战斗团体） || 文化联想：在北京动物园里看到那种胸背宽厚、手臂粗壮、体型远大于猴子的非洲大猩猩，它就是 gorilla；这个词指的就是“大猩猩”，不需要拿中国本土动物去硬类比，可以说 **a gorilla — “Visitors to a Chinese zoo can easily distinguish a gorilla from smaller monkeys by its massive build and long arms.”**

quiz.question: parabola _____
quiz.explanation: 抛物线，抛物线曲线。The mathematics teacher explained the parabola curve. 数学老师解释了抛物线曲线。 | para->旁边，bol->投掷（希腊ballein），parabola->投掷旁边的曲线=抛物线（cf. parable寓言，symbol象征，hyperbole夸张=过度投掷） || 文化联想：中国学生做高考数学时最熟悉的 y=x² 那条开口向上的曲线，就是标准的 parabola，可以说 **a parabola — “The graph of y = x² forms a parabola familiar to generations of Chinese students.”**

quiz.question: ________ formula
quiz.explanation: 公式，化学公式。The chemist wrote the chemical formula on the board. 化学家在黑板上写下化学公式。 | form->形式（拉丁forma），formula->小形式=表达规则的格式（cf. formal正式，reform改革，inform通知，uniform制服） || 文化联想：《伤寒论》里的经典方剂讲究固定药味和配伍比例，从“按规则组合而成的配方”这一层意思看，很容易帮助理解 formula，可以说 **a traditional medicinal formula — “A prescription recorded in the Shanghan Lun can be understood as a traditional medicinal formula.”**

quiz.question: _______ peninsula
quiz.explanation: 半岛，伊比利亚半岛。Spain and Portugal are located on the Iberian peninsula. 西班牙和葡萄牙位于伊比利亚半岛上。 | paene->几乎（拉丁），insula->岛，peninsula->几乎是岛=半岛（cf. island岛，insulate绝缘，penury赤贫=几乎没有，penultimate倒数第二） || 文化联想：山东三面临海、只有西侧与大陆相连，典型体现了 peninsula“几乎像岛、但仍与大陆相接”的地理特征，可以说 **the Shandong Peninsula — “The Shandong Peninsula is surrounded by sea on three sides and connected to the mainland on the west.”**

quiz.question: _______ spatula
quiz.explanation: 铲子，厨房铲子。She used a kitchen spatula to flip the pancakes. 她用厨房铲子翻煎饼。 | spat->宽扁（拉丁spatha->宽剑），spatula->小宽扁工具=铲子（cf. spade铁锹，spadix花序，epaulet肩章=小肩膀） || 文化联想：中式炒菜时用来铲菜、翻炒、刮锅底的扁平锅铲，就是最直观的 spatula，可以说 **a wok spatula — “A cook uses a wok spatula to toss, turn, and scrape food during stir-frying.”**

quiz.question: ______ melodrama
quiz.explanation: 情节剧，家庭情节剧。The TV show was a typical family melodrama. 这个电视节目是典型的家庭情节剧。 | melo->歌曲（希腊melos），drama->戏剧，melodrama->有音乐的戏剧=情节剧（cf. melody旋律，dramatic戏剧性，drama戏剧） || 文化联想：传统苦情电视剧里常见失散、误会、绝症、哭喊轮番上阵，把情绪和冲突推到极致，这种夸张煽情的戏剧风格就是 melodrama，可以说 **a melodrama — “A tear-soaked family drama full of improbable twists can become pure melodrama.”**

quiz.question: ________ panorama
quiz.explanation: 全景，山景全景。The lookout offered a breathtaking mountain panorama. 瞭望台提供了令人惊叹的山景全景。 | pan->全部（希腊），horama->景象（希腊horan->看），panorama->全面的景象=全景（cf. pantheism泛神，pandemic全球流行，panoramic全景的） || 文化联想：《清明上河图》长卷缓缓展开时，城门、街市、河道和人群连续铺陈，像把汴京生活一览无余地呈现在眼前；这种“整体尽收眼底”的视野就是 panorama，可以说 **a panorama — “The long scroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival offers a panorama of urban life in the Northern Song capital.”**

quiz.question: _____ anathema
quiz.explanation: 诅咒，彻底的诅咒。Such behavior was utter anathema to their beliefs. 这种行为对他们的信仰来说是彻底的诅咒。 | ana->向上，thema->放置（希腊），anathema->放上去献祭/诅咒=诅咒（cf. theme主题，theorem定理，hypothesis假设=放置在下） || 文化联想：在传统宗族伦理里，“忤逆不孝”常被视为最不能容忍、人人避之的行为；这种被群体强烈厌恶、几乎视为禁忌的东西可以用 anathema 来形容，可以说 **anathema — “In a strict traditional clan, open disrespect toward one's parents might be treated as anathema.”**

quiz.question: _________ dogma
quiz.explanation: 教条，宗教教条。The sect followed strict religious dogma. 这个教派遵循严格的宗教教条。 | dogma->信念（希腊dokein->认为），dogma->被认定的教义=教条（cf. dogmatic武断的，orthodox正统，doctrine教义，paradox悖论） || 文化联想：如果把“三纲五常”当成绝不能质疑、只能照搬的绝对准则，它就体现了 dogma 的意味：被僵硬奉为真理的教条，可以说 **dogma — “When moral maxims are treated as unquestionable truth, they harden into dogma.”**

quiz.question: asthma ______
quiz.explanation: 哮喘，哮喘发作。She carried an inhaler in case of an asthma attack. 她随身携带吸入器以防哮喘发作。 | asthma->喘息（希腊azein->喘），asthma->呼吸困难的病（cf. aeration通气，aspirate吸气，aerobic有氧） || 文化联想：春季花粉或冷空气一刺激，有些人会反复喘鸣、胸闷、呼吸困难，这种慢性气道疾病就是 asthma，可以说 **asthma — “Cold air and spring pollen can trigger asthma in susceptible people.”**

quiz.question: _____ dilemma
quiz.explanation: 困境，道德困境。The doctor faced a difficult moral dilemma. 医生面临着困难的道德困境。 | di->两个（希腊），lemma->前提/选择（希腊），dilemma->两个前提的困境（cf. trilemma三难困境，lemma引理，double bind双重束缚） || 文化联想：中国传统故事常说“忠孝不能两全”：无论选忠还是选孝都要牺牲另一边，这种两头为难、没有轻松答案的处境就是 dilemma，可以说 **a dilemma — “The conflict between loyalty to the state and filial duty can create a painful dilemma.”**

quiz.question: ______ comma
quiz.explanation: 逗号，牛津逗号。Writers debate whether to use the Oxford comma. 作家们争论是否使用牛津逗号。 | komma->切断（希腊koptein->切），comma->切断句子的标记=逗号（cf. colon结肠/冒号，semicolon分号，period句号） || 文化联想：现代人给古文加标点时，会用逗号标出句中较短的停顿；古人虽靠“句读”断句，但今天那个弯弯的小停顿符号就是 comma，可以说 **a comma — “Modern punctuation inserts a comma where a reader of classical Chinese might make a short pause.”**

quiz.question: ____ ____ coma
quiz.explanation: 昏迷，陷入昏迷。The patient would fall into coma after the accident. 患者会在事故后陷入昏迷。 | koma->深睡（希腊），coma->深度无意识状态=昏迷（cf. comma逗号同根，somnolent困倦，sedation镇静） || 文化联想：武侠故事里人物中毒或重伤后长时间不省人事、怎么呼唤都没有清醒反应，这种深度无意识状态就是 coma，可以说 **a coma — “A badly injured hero who remains unconscious for days has fallen into a coma.”**

quiz.question: ____ aroma
quiz.explanation: 香味，浓郁的香味。The coffee had a rich aroma that filled the room. 咖啡有浓郁的香味弥漫整个房间。 | aroma->香料（希腊，来自东方香料），aroma->令人愉快的气味（cf. aromatic芳香的，aromatherapy香薰疗法，spice香料） || 文化联想：刚揭开一锅重庆火锅或广式老火汤的锅盖，香味一下子弥漫整个屋子；这种令人愉快、能明显闻到的香气就是 aroma，可以说 **aroma — “The aroma of a simmering hotpot can fill an entire room before the lid is lifted.”**

quiz.question: _____ miasma
quiz.explanation: 瘴气，有毒的瘴气。A toxic miasma rose from the swamp. 有毒的瘴气从沼泽升起。 | miasma->污染（希腊miainein->污染），miasma->有毒的瘴气（中世纪认为瘴气致病，malaria=mal+aria=坏空气，cf. miasmatic瘴气的） || 文化联想：古籍常把岭南、云南湿热山区描写成“瘴疠之地”，认为山林间有会致病的瘴气；这种旧观念中的有害浊气正对应 miasma，可以说 **miasma — “Old accounts of southern frontier regions often blamed disease on a poisonous miasma rising from the landscape.”**

quiz.question: ________ charisma
quiz.explanation: 魅力，磁性的魅力。The leader had magnetic charisma that attracted followers. 领导者有磁性的魅力吸引追随者。 | charis->恩典（希腊），charisma->神赐的魅力（cf. grace恩典，charity慈善，charismatic有魅力，eucharist圣餐=感恩） || 文化联想：《水浒传》里宋江并非武艺最强，却能让许多好汉愿意聚拢追随；这种单靠个人号召力就能吸引他人的特质，很容易让人联想到 charisma，可以说 **personal charisma — “Song Jiang's ability to attract followers despite not being the strongest fighter reflects personal charisma.”**

quiz.question: _______ phenomena
quiz.explanation: 现象，自然现象。Scientists study natural phenomena to understand the world. 科学家研究自然现象以了解世界。 | phainomenon->出现的事物（希腊），phenomena->多个现象（cf. phenomenon单数，phenomenal非凡，phantom幻影，fantasy幻想） || 文化联想：古人制定二十四节气，就是长期观察雷鸣、霜降、候鸟迁徙、草木萌发等反复出现的自然表现；这些可观察到的现象就是 phenomena，可以说 **seasonal phenomena — “The twenty-four solar terms were built around recurring seasonal phenomena observed over generations.”**

quiz.question: _____ _ subpoena
quiz.explanation: 传票，送达传票。The court officer would serve a subpoena to the witness. 法庭官员会向证人送达传票。 | sub->在...下，poena->惩罚（拉丁），subpoena->在惩罚威胁下=传票（cf. pain痛苦，penal惩罚，penalty罚款，punish惩罚） || 文化联想：古代衙门派差役送到当事人手里的传唤文书，要求其按时到堂接受询问；在现代法律概念上最容易帮助理解 subpoena，可以说 **a subpoena — “A modern court can compel a witness to appear by issuing a subpoena.”**

quiz.question: ______ ballerina
quiz.explanation: 芭蕾舞女演员，芭蕾舞女演员。The graceful ballet ballerina performed beautifully. 优雅的芭蕾舞女演员表演得很美。 | ballare->舞蹈（意大利语，希腊ballizein->跳），ballerina->女舞者（cf. ballet芭蕾，ball舞会，balloon气球=圆球） || 文化联想：芭蕾舞剧《红色娘子军》里穿足尖鞋完成旋转和跳跃的女舞者，就是中国观众很熟悉的 ballerina 形象，可以说 **a ballerina in The Red Detachment of Women — “A ballerina in The Red Detachment of Women combines classical ballet technique with a distinctly Chinese revolutionary story.”**

quiz.question: _____ patina
quiz.explanation: 铜绿，绿色铜绿。The old bronze statue had a green patina. 旧青铜雕像有绿色铜绿。 | patina->浅盘（拉丁patina->平锅），patina->金属表面的薄层氧化=铜绿（cf. pan平底锅，paten圣餐盘，patina of age岁月痕迹） || 文化联想：故宫里的老铜器和古董家具表面经过多年氧化、摩挲后形成的铜绿或温润包浆，都可以让人理解 patina：岁月留在表面的薄层痕迹，可以说 **the patina of age — “The patina of age on an old bronze vessel can make centuries of history visible on its surface.”**

quiz.question: __ antenna
quiz.explanation: 天线，电视天线。They adjusted the TV antenna to improve reception. 他们调整电视天线以改善接收。 | antenna->斜桁（拉丁，帆船上的横杆），antenna->昆虫触角/无线电天线（cf. antenna昆虫的触须，broadcast广播，reception接收） || 文化联想：过去家里老式电视机顶上那两根可以掰来掰去找信号的“兔耳朵”，就是 antenna，可以说 **a rabbit-ear antenna — “Families once adjusted a rabbit-ear antenna on top of the television to improve reception.”**

quiz.question: penumbra __ _____
quiz.explanation: 半影，疑云的半影。A penumbra of doubt surrounded the decision. 疑云的半影笼罩着这个决定。 | paene->几乎（拉丁），umbra->影子，penumbra->几乎是影子=半影（cf. umbrella雨伞=小影子，umbrage生气=被阴影笼罩，adumbrate概述） || 文化联想：发生半影月食时，月亮进入地球影子的较淡外层，亮度只是悄悄变暗；那片不完全黑暗的影区就是 penumbra，可以说 **Earth's penumbra — “During a penumbral lunar eclipse, the Moon passes through Earth's penumbra and dims only slightly.”**

quiz.question: ______ tundra
quiz.explanation: 苔原，冰冻的苔原。The Arctic frozen tundra is a harsh environment. 北极冰冻的苔原是严酷的环境。 | tundra->山上平原（芬兰语tunturi->平顶山），tundra->北极无树平原=苔原（cf. taiga针叶林带，permafrost永久冻土） || 文化联想：青藏高原一些极高寒地区几乎长不出乔木，只剩低矮草本、苔藓和地衣，这种寒冷、无树的植被地带可以让人联想到 tundra，可以说 **alpine tundra — “Treeless high-altitude regions of the Tibetan Plateau can resemble alpine tundra.”**

quiz.question: ____ chimera
quiz.explanation: 幻想，狂野的幻想。His plan was just a wild chimera with no basis in reality. 他的计划只是没有现实基础的狂野的幻想。 | Chimaira->希腊神话狮头羊身蛇尾怪兽，chimera->不可能实现的幻想（cf. chimerical荒诞的，chimeric基因嵌合体） || 文化联想：中国龙把鹿角、蛇身、鹰爪等多种动物特征组合在一个神兽形象上；从“由不同生物特征拼合而成的怪兽”这一点看，它很像 chimera，可以说 **a chimera-like creature — “The Chinese dragon is a chimera-like creature assembled from features associated with several different animals.”**

quiz.question: _ plethora __
quiz.explanation: 过剩，过剩的。The store offered a plethora of choices. 商店提供了过剩的选择。 | plethora->充满（希腊plethein->充满），plethora->过多=过剩（cf. plentiful充裕，replete充满，plenty充足，complete完整） || 文化联想：走进义乌国际商贸城，发夹、玩具、五金、饰品一眼望不到头，选择多到让人无从下手，这种“多得过头”的丰富就是 plethora，可以说 **plethora — “The Yiwu market offers a plethora of small goods in almost every imaginable category.”**

quiz.question: ______ flora
quiz.explanation: 植物群，高山植物群。Botanists study the unique alpine flora. 植物学家研究独特的高山植物群。 | Flora->罗马花神，flora->某地区的植物总称（cf. flower花，flourish繁荣，floral花卉的，fauna动物群=与flora对应） || 文化联想：云南被称为“植物王国”，从热带雨林到高山杜鹃，不同海拔分布着极丰富的植物种类；一个地区全部植物的总称就是 flora，可以说 **the flora of Yunnan — “The flora of Yunnan ranges from tropical plants to alpine rhododendrons.”**

quiz.question: ________ orchestra
quiz.explanation: 管弦乐队，交响乐团。The symphony orchestra performed Beethoven. 交响乐团演奏了贝多芬的作品。 | orkhestra->舞蹈的地方（希腊，古剧场合唱队站的区域），orchestra->乐队演奏区=管弦乐队（cf. orchestrate精心安排，choreography编舞） || 文化联想：中国民族乐团里二胡、琵琶、笛子、唢呐和打击乐等许多声部由指挥统一演奏，这样的大型器乐合奏团就是 orchestra 的中国式对应场景，可以说 **a Chinese orchestra — “A Chinese orchestra brings instruments such as the erhu, pipa, dizi, and suona together under one conductor.”**

quiz.question: bravura ___________
